transcript.speaker: William Brown
transcript.content: Hi Esmeralda — do you have a minute? I'm feeling a bit torn about my 5-year-old niece: at family gatherings she's pretty demanding and attention-seeking, and I catch myself getting annoyed, which then makes me feel guilty. I want to stay close to her without creating more family tension—do you have any advice on how I can connect with her or manage my reactions?

transcript.speaker: Esmeralda Solis
transcript.content: I hear you — feeling annoyed and guilty at the same time is totally normal with a lively five‑year‑old. Often that attention‑seeking is a plea for connection or predictability, so try short, regular one‑on‑one rituals (10–15 minutes of dancing or a game), offer simple choices, and set calm, consistent limits. A quick line that works: “I want to play with you — I can in five minutes; would you like to draw or dance while we wait?” — also agree with her caregivers on a signal you can use to step away when you’re overwhelmed.

transcript.speaker: William Brown
transcript.content: Thanks, Esmeralda — that actually helps. I like the idea of a short dance or game ritual; since we both love dancing I could try a 10‑minute dance break as our thing. Do you have a practical way to agree on a signal with the caregivers without sounding like I’m shirking responsibility? And any tips to make the “I can play in five minutes” line feel sincere instead of dismissive?

transcript.speaker: Esmeralda Solis
transcript.content: I'd suggest agreeing privately with the caregivers on a neutral, positive signal — a small colored card, a gentle hand on your chest, or a whispered word — and present it to her as “our special pause sign” so it reads as structure, not shirking. To make “I can play in five minutes” feel sincere, get down to her level, name her feeling (“I know you really want to play”), offer a concrete choice (pick the song or the game), and use a visible timer or quick countdown so she can see you’ll come back — then follow through. That predictability and the brief one‑on‑one ritual will build trust and help you step away without guilt.

transcript.speaker: William Brown
transcript.content: Thanks, Esmeralda — that feels doable. Could you help me with a short script I can use with the caregivers to introduce the “special pause” and a simple line I can say to her that sounds sincere when I use it? Also, any quick strategy you use to quiet the guilt in the moment if I still get annoyed?

transcript.speaker: Esmeralda Solis
transcript.content:
Try this short script with the caregivers: “Could we agree on a small ‘special pause’ signal — like a colored card or a gentle tap — that means I need two minutes to regroup? During that pause, can you offer her a quick choice (pick a song or draw) and I’ll come back for our 10‑minute dance?”

A sincere line to the niece (get down to her level and use her name): “I know you really want to play right now — I can in five minutes. Would you like to pick the song we’ll dance to or draw while we wait? I’ll set the timer and come right back.”

To quiet the guilt in the moment: take three slow breaths, name the purpose (“I’m doing this so I can be present with her”), and remind yourself that predictable limits build trust — then follow through so the next pause feels safe for both of you.

transcript.speaker: William Brown
transcript.content: This is really helpful — thank you, I’ll try the 10‑minute dance and use the timer and pause signal. Quick favor: if I do lose my temper and snap, what’s a very short, sincere repair line I can say right away to her to make it better?

transcript.speaker: Esmeralda Solis
transcript.content: If you snap, try a very short repair like: “I’m sorry I yelled — that was my fault. You’re not in trouble; I was frustrated. Give me two minutes to calm down and then we’ll have our dance — do you want to pick the song?” Get down to her level, say it calmly, follow through on the pause, and offer a hug if she wants one.
